title: Gold complexes as systems-disruptive anticancer agents: beyond thioredoxin reductase inhibition
content: Gold-based compounds have re-emerged as a distinct class of metal-based therapeutics whose biological activity is fundamentally shaped by chemically encoded polypharmacology rather than single-target inhibition. In contrast to classical platinum drugs that act primarily through direct DNA damage, gold complexes exert their effects predominantly at the protein level, exploiting the strong affinity of gold complexes for cysteine and selenocysteine residues. While inhibition of thioredoxin reductase (TrxR) is a recurring molecular entry point in gold pharmacology, additional direct interactions and downstream effects contribute to biological activity in a compound- and context-dependent manner. This review advances a systems-level framework in which the so-called secondary targets of gold, encompassing redox enzymes, metabolic regulators, proteostatic machinery, signalling mediators, and structural proteins, are considered as potentially interconnected components of the pharmacological response. By perturbing redox homeostasis, mitochondrial function, protein quality control, adaptive signalling, and cellular architecture, gold complexes may generate cumulative cellular stress that can exceed the adaptive capacity of cancer cells. The proposed model may help rationalize the anticancer activity and synergy with targeted therapies reported for selected gold compounds, while providing a basis for investigating whether perturbation of multiple cellular pathways can limit resistance development. By critically integrating current mechanistic insights, this review reframes gold complexes as system-disruptive agents and outlines how this perspective can guide the rational design of next-generation gold-based therapeutics. Emphasis is placed on exploiting controlled polyreactivity, ligand-directed signalling bias, and combination strategies that leverage network fragility, thereby positioning gold chemistry as a model for systems-oriented drug design in medicinal inorganic chemistry. This perspective challenges the prevailing single-target paradigm in medicinal inorganic chemistry.
